title: IAM & Security
subtitle: Users, roles, policies, and least-privilege access — the security foundation every AWS account must get right

content.text: IAM — the gatekeeper of your AWS account

IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the service that controls who can do what in your AWS account. Every API call to AWS — whether from the console, CLI, or your application code — is checked against IAM policies before it's allowed. Getting IAM right is the single most important thing you can do for AWS security.

content.code:
1. USERS — A person or application with long-term credentials
   - Has a username + password (for console access)
   - Has an Access Key ID + Secret Access Key (for CLI/SDK access)
   - Example: 'alice' (a developer), 'deploy-bot' (a CI/CD service account)
   ⚠  Never use root user for daily work — create IAM users instead

2. GROUPS — A collection of users with shared permissions
   - 'Developers' group → can read/write S3 and EC2
   - 'Admins' group → full access
   - Assign a user to a group instead of attaching policies to each user

3. ROLES — A temporary identity that can be assumed
   - An EC2 instance assumes a role to access S3 without storing credentials
   - A Lambda function assumes a role to write to DynamoDB
   - A GitHub Actions workflow assumes a role to deploy to ECS
   ✓ Preferred over users for application/service access — no long-term secrets

4. POLICIES — JSON documents that define permissions
   - Attached to users, groups, or roles
   - Allow or Deny specific actions on specific resources

content.text: Grant only the minimum permissions needed to perform a task. A Lambda function that reads from DynamoDB should have dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:Query permissions on that specific table — not dynamodb:* on all tables, and definitely not *:* (full admin). This limits the blast radius if credentials are ever compromised.

content.filename: Securing your root account — critical first steps
content.code:
# Day 1 AWS security checklist:

# 1. NEVER use root for daily work
#    Root: the god account created when you sign up
#    Create an IAM admin user for yourself, then don't touch root

# 2. Enable MFA on root (and all IAM users)
#    AWS Console → IAM → Security credentials → MFA

# 3. Don't create root access keys
#    If they exist, delete them immediately

# 4. Create IAM users for people, roles for services
#    Never put AWS credentials in code or environment variables
#    on servers — use IAM roles instead

# 5. Use IAM Access Analyzer to find over-permissive policies
aws accessanalyzer list-analyzers

# 6. Enable CloudTrail (audit log of all API calls)
#    Free for management events — see who did what and when
aws cloudtrail describe-trails

content.text: Never commit AWS credentials to git. Access Key IDs and Secret Access Keys in a public GitHub repository are scraped by bots within minutes. The attacker spins up EC2 instances for crypto mining, and you get a $10,000 AWS bill. Use IAM roles for services, aws configure for local dev (stores in ~/.aws/credentials), and environment secrets for CI/CD. If you accidentally commit credentials, delete the key in IAM immediately, then rotate all affected secrets.

questions.question: Your Node.js app running on EC2 needs to upload files to S3. What is the correct way to give it access?
options: Set AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID and AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY environment variables on the EC2 instance
Hardcode the credentials in the Node.js source code
Create an IAM role with S3 PutObject permission, attach it to the EC2 instance — no credentials needed in code
Add the IAM user's credentials to a .env file on the server
questions.explanation: IAM roles for EC2 instances (called 'instance profiles') are the correct approach. The EC2 instance automatically receives temporary, rotating credentials from the IAM role via the instance metadata service. The AWS SDK reads these automatically — no credential configuration in code or environment variables. Options A, B, and D all involve long-lived credentials that could be exposed via a file read, env dump, or git commit.

faq.q: What is the difference between IAM policies and S3 bucket policies?
faq.a: IAM policies are attached to identities (users, roles) and say what that identity can do. S3 bucket policies are attached to the bucket and say who can access that bucket. They work together: both must allow for access to succeed (unless one is explicitly denied). Bucket policies are necessary for cross-account access or allowing public read access to a bucket.

examples: Capital One's 2019 data breach exposed 100 million records due to a misconfigured WAF that allowed an SSRF attack to reach the EC2 metadata service and retrieve IAM role credentials. The role had too-broad S3 permissions — a least-privilege policy would have contained the blast radius

IAM Identity Center (formerly SSO) lets teams log into multiple AWS accounts with one set of credentials, assigning different roles per account — developers get read-only in production, full access in dev
